lines.say: Take an example: a four hundred thousand dollar loan at seven point four percent, Freddie Mac's average rate on October eighth, twenty twenty-six.

lines.say: The first payment is two thousand seven hundred sixty-nine dollars and fifty-two cents. About two thousand four hundred sixty-seven is interest. Only about three hundred three pays down the loan.

lines.text: Chapter 1: The parts of a mortgage
lines.say: Chapter one: the parts of a mortgage.

lines.text: A mortgage is a loan to buy a home, and the home itself is the collateral.
lines.say: A mortgage is a loan to buy a home, and the home itself is the collateral.

lines.text: Principal is what you borrow. Our example: $400,000 on a $500,000 home with 20% down.
lines.say: Three basics. The principal is what you borrow. In our example, four hundred thousand dollars, on a five hundred thousand dollar home with twenty percent down.

lines.text: The interest rate is the yearly price of borrowing it. Here, 7.40%.
lines.say: The interest rate is the yearly price of borrowing it. Here, seven point four percent.

lines.text: The term is how long you have to pay it back. The US standard is 30 years.
lines.say: And the term is how long you have to repay. The US standard is thirty years.

lines.text: But loan offers show two percentages: the interest rate and the APR.
lines.say: But loan offers show two percentages: the interest rate and the A P R.

lines.text: Per the CFPB, APR is the rate plus points, broker fees and other charges, as one yearly rate.
lines.say: Per the C F P B, the A P R is the rate plus points, broker fees and other charges, as one yearly rate.

lines.text: Example: $8,000 of lender fees turns a 7.40% rate into about a 7.61% APR.
lines.say: In our example, eight thousand dollars of lender fees turns seven point four percent into an A P R of about seven point six one percent.

lines.text: So APR helps compare offers. A low rate with big fees can cost more than it looks.
lines.say: So the A P R helps compare offers. A low rate with big fees can cost more than it looks.

lines.text: Points are fees paid up front for a lower rate. One point is 1% of the loan.
lines.say: Then there are points: fees paid up front for a lower rate. One point is one percent of the loan.

lines.text: On $400,000, one point costs $4,000.
lines.say: So on our loan, one point costs four thousand dollars.

lines.text: The rate cut per point varies. Say 7.15%: the payment falls $67.89 a month.
lines.say: How much a point cuts the rate varies. Say it's seven point one five percent. The payment falls from about two thousand seven hundred seventy to about two thousand seven hundred two, or sixty-seven dollars and eighty-nine cents a month.

lines.text: $4,000 / $67.89 = about 59 months, roughly 5 years, to break even. Sell or refinance sooner, and the point cost more than it saved.
lines.say: Divide four thousand by that, and you break even in about fifty-nine months, roughly five years. Sell or refinance sooner, and the point cost more than it saved.

lines.text: Chapter 2: The payment math
lines.say: Chapter two: the payment math.

lines.text: Every fixed-rate payment comes from one formula. It's friendlier than it looks.
lines.say: Every fixed-rate payment comes from one formula, and it's friendlier than it looks.

lines.text: L is the loan, r the monthly rate, n the number of payments.
lines.say: L is the loan, r is the monthly rate, and n is the number of payments.

lines.text: Monthly payment: $2,769.52, the same for all 30 years. What changes is what's inside it.
lines.say: The payment comes out to two thousand seven hundred sixty-nine dollars and fifty-two cents, the same for thirty years. What changes is what's inside it.

lines.text: Interest = balance x rate / 12. Month one: $400,000 x 7.40% / 12 = $2,466.67.
lines.say: Each month's interest is the balance times the rate, over twelve. In month one, that's two thousand four hundred sixty-six dollars and sixty-seven cents.

lines.text: The rest pays down principal: $2,769.52 - $2,466.67 = $302.85.
lines.say: The rest pays down principal: three hundred two dollars and eighty-five cents.

lines.text: So after one payment, the balance only drops to $399,697.
lines.say: So after one payment, the balance only drops to three hundred ninety-nine thousand, six hundred ninety-seven.

lines.text: Next month, interest is figured on a slightly smaller balance, so a bit more goes to principal. That's amortization.
lines.say: Next month, interest is figured on a slightly smaller balance, so a bit more goes to principal. That slow shift is amortization.

lines.text: Year one: $29,474 of interest, just $3,760 of principal.
lines.say: Year one adds up to about twenty-nine thousand four hundred seventy-four dollars of interest, and just three thousand seven hundred sixty of principal.

lines.text: The balance falls slowly at first, then faster near the end.
lines.say: Here's the balance over time. It falls slowly at first, then faster near the end.

lines.text: After 10 years and about $332,000 of payments, you'd still owe $346,411.
lines.say: After ten years and about three hundred thirty-two thousand dollars of payments, you'd still owe three hundred forty-six thousand, four hundred eleven.

lines.text: Only $53,589 of the loan is paid off.
lines.say: Only fifty-three thousand, five hundred eighty-nine dollars is paid off.

lines.text: Principal finally beats interest at payment 249, in year 21.
lines.say: Principal doesn't beat interest until payment two forty-nine, in year twenty-one.

lines.text: Why? Interest is charged on what you owe, and early on, you owe almost all of it.
lines.say: Why so slow? Interest is charged on what you owe, and early on, you owe almost all of it.

lines.text: Over 30 years: about $997,000 in total. $400K of loan, about $597K of interest.
lines.say: Over thirty years, that's about nine hundred ninety-seven thousand dollars in total: four hundred thousand of loan, about five hundred ninety-seven thousand of interest.

lines.text: Now a 15-year loan. On Oct 8, 2026, Freddie Mac's 15-year average was 6.73%.
lines.say: Now a fifteen-year loan. On October eighth, twenty twenty-six, Freddie Mac's fifteen-year average was six point seven three percent.

lines.text: Same $400,000: about $3,535 a month versus about $2,770.
lines.say: Same loan: about three thousand five hundred thirty-five dollars a month, versus about two thousand seven hundred seventy.

lines.text: But total interest drops to about $236K, roughly $361K less.
lines.say: But total interest drops to about two hundred thirty-six thousand dollars, roughly three hundred sixty-one thousand less.

lines.text: Lower rate, half the time, far less interest. The trade-off is a much bigger monthly bill.
lines.say: Lower rate, half the time, far less interest. The trade-off is a much bigger monthly bill.

lines.text: Some pick 30 years for the lower payment; others pick 15 to build equity fast.
lines.say: Some people pick thirty years for the lower payment. Others pick fifteen to build equity fast. Both are just math.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Where your rate comes from
lines.say: Chapter three: where your rate comes from.

lines.text: The rate on the news usually comes from Freddie Mac's weekly survey, the PMMS.
lines.say: The rate on the news usually comes from Freddie Mac's weekly survey, the P M M S.

lines.text: It averages conventional loans for borrowers with 20% down and excellent credit.
lines.say: It's the average for borrowers with twenty percent down and excellent credit.

lines.text: The yearly average 30-year rate, 2016 to 2025, ending at about 6.6%.
lines.say: Here's the yearly average thirty-year rate from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-five, ending at about six point six percent.

lines.text: It bottomed out at a 2.96% average in 2021.
lines.say: It bottomed out in twenty twenty-one, at two point nine six percent.

lines.text: Then it more than doubled, to 6.81% in 2023.
lines.say: Then it more than doubled, to six point eight one percent in twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: Our loan: about $1,678 a month at 2.96%, versus about $2,770 at 7.40%.
lines.say: On our loan, that's about one thousand six hundred seventy-eight dollars a month at the twenty twenty-one rate, versus about two thousand seven hundred seventy at seven point four.

lines.text: The survey's record high was 18.63%, in October 1981.
lines.say: The survey's record high was eighteen point six three percent, in October nineteen eighty-one.

lines.text: Its record low was 2.65%, in January 2021.
lines.say: Its record low was two point six five percent, in January twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: On Oct 8, 2026, it was 7.40%, up from 5.98% in late February 2026.
lines.say: On October eighth, twenty twenty-six, it was seven point four percent, up from five point nine eight in late February.

lines.text: A new number comes out almost every Thursday, and nobody knows which way it goes next.
lines.say: A new number comes out almost every Thursday, and nobody knows which way it goes next.

lines.text: Your own rate can differ: lenders price in credit score, down payment, loan type and points.
lines.say: Your own rate can differ. Lenders price in your credit score, down payment, loan type and points.

lines.text: The 2026 conforming loan limit: $832,750 for a one-unit home in most areas (FHFA).
lines.say: Then there's the conforming loan limit. For twenty twenty-six, it's eight hundred thirty-two thousand, seven hundred fifty dollars in most areas.

lines.text: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can buy loans up to it. Bigger ones are jumbo loans. FHFA resets it yearly.
lines.say: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can buy loans up to that limit. Bigger ones are jumbo loans. F H F A resets it every year.

lines.text: For scale: the median existing home sold for $417,500 in September 2026 (NAR).
lines.say: For scale, the median existing home sold for four hundred seventeen thousand, five hundred dollars in September twenty twenty-six, according to the National Association of Realtors.

lines.text: Chapter 4: PITI, the full monthly bill
lines.say: Chapter four: PITI, the full monthly bill.

lines.text: That $2,769.52 payment is only P and I: principal and interest.
lines.say: That payment we figured is only the P and the I: principal and interest.

lines.text: Lenders usually add a T and another I: property taxes and homeowners insurance.
lines.say: Lenders usually add a T and another I: property taxes and homeowners insurance.

lines.text: ATTOM: the average effective property tax rate on single-family homes was 0.9% in 2025.
lines.say: Taxes first. The data firm ATTOM put the average effective property tax rate on single-family homes at zero point nine percent in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: It varies a lot. Illinois led at 1.84%, then New Jersey at 1.58%.
lines.say: It varies a lot. Illinois led at one point eight four percent, then New Jersey at one point five eight.

lines.text: Our $500,000 home at 0.9%: $4,500 a year, or $375 a month.
lines.say: On our five hundred thousand dollar home, that's four thousand five hundred dollars a year, or three hundred seventy-five a month.

lines.text: Bankrate: the average homeowners policy is $2,424 a year for $300,000 of dwelling coverage.
lines.say: For insurance, Bankrate's national average is two thousand four hundred twenty-four dollars a year, for three hundred thousand dollars of dwelling coverage.

lines.text: That's $202 a month. Lenders require it, because the house secures their loan.
lines.say: That's two hundred two dollars a month. Lenders require it, because the house secures their loan.
Add it all up, and the real monthly bill is three thousand three hundred forty-six dollars and fifty-two cents.

lines.text: That's about 21% more than the payment people usually quote.
lines.say: That's about twenty-one percent more than the payment people usually quote.

lines.text: Taxes and insurance usually run through escrow: the servicer collects monthly and pays the bills.
lines.say: Taxes and insurance usually run through escrow. The servicer collects a slice each month and pays those bills.

lines.text: Federal rules cap the cushion at 1/6 of the yearly total, about 2 months.
lines.say: Federal rules cap its cushion at one sixth of the yearly total, about two months.

lines.text: It's reviewed yearly. If taxes or insurance rise, so does the payment, even on a fixed rate.
lines.say: It's reviewed every year. If taxes or insurance rise, so does the payment, even on a fixed rate.

lines.text: Under 20% down on a conventional loan, you usually pay private mortgage insurance, or PMI.
lines.say: Next up, P M I. Put under twenty percent down on a conventional loan, and you usually pay private mortgage insurance.

lines.text: It protects the lender. Freddie Mac: typically $30 to $70 a month per $100,000 borrowed.
lines.say: It protects the lender, not you. Freddie Mac says it typically runs thirty to seventy dollars a month per hundred thousand borrowed.

lines.text: Example: same home, 10% down. A $450,000 loan, PMI of about $135 to $315 a month.
lines.say: Example: same home, ten percent down. That's a four hundred fifty thousand dollar loan, and roughly one hundred thirty-five to three hundred fifteen a month of P M I.

lines.text: The part most people never hear: a 1998 law sets when PMI must end.
lines.say: Here's what most people never hear. A nineteen ninety-eight law, the Homeowners Protection Act, sets when it must end.

lines.text: At 80% of the original value, you can ask to cancel it, with a good payment record.
lines.say: At eighty percent of the home's original value, you can ask to cancel it, with a good payment record.

lines.text: At 78% on the original schedule, the servicer must drop it automatically, if you're current.
lines.say: At seventy-eight percent on the original schedule, the servicer must drop it automatically, if you're current.

lines.text: Otherwise, it ends at the loan's halfway point, if you're current.
lines.say: Otherwise, it ends at the loan's halfway point, if you're current.

lines.text: On the $450,000 loan: 80% comes at payment 105; 78% at payment 120, exactly 10 years.
lines.say: On our four hundred fifty thousand dollar example, eighty percent comes at payment one oh five, and seventy-eight percent at payment one twenty: exactly ten years.

lines.text: Extra payments reach 80% sooner. FHA, VA and USDA loans have their own rules.
lines.say: Extra payments can reach eighty percent sooner. And F H A, V A and U S D A loans follow their own rules, not this law.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Getting the loan
lines.say: Chapter five: getting the loan.

lines.text: Closing costs typically run 2% to 5% of the purchase price.
lines.say: Closing costs typically run two to five percent of the purchase price.

lines.text: On a $500,000 home: $10,000 to $25,000, for appraisal, title, lender fees and points.
lines.say: On our home, that's ten thousand to twenty-five thousand dollars, for the appraisal, title, lender fees and points.

lines.text: Loan Estimate: within 3 business days of applying. Closing Disclosure: 3 business days before closing.
lines.say: Lenders must send a Loan Estimate within three business days of applying, and a Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing.

lines.text: A fixed-rate loan keeps one rate for the whole term. An adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM, can change.
lines.say: Fixed-rate loans keep one rate for the whole term. An adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM, can change.

lines.text: A 5/6 ARM is fixed for 5 years, then adjusts every 6 months.
lines.say: A five six ARM is fixed for five years, then adjusts every six months.

lines.text: The new rate = an index, usually SOFR, plus a margin set in the loan.
lines.say: The new rate is an index, usually SOFR, plus a margin set in the loan.

lines.text: Common 2/1/5 caps: +2 points at the first change, +1 after that, +5 for life.
lines.say: Common two, one, five caps allow up to two points at the first change, one point after that, and five points over the life of the loan.

lines.text: Hypothetical: start at 6%, and it could hit 8% at the first change, never above 11%.
lines.say: So an ARM starting at six percent could hit eight percent at the first change, and never top eleven.

lines.text: After the fixed period, the payment can rise, and nobody knows rates 5 years out.
lines.say: After the fixed period, the payment can rise, and nobody knows rates five years out.

lines.text: Last number: DTI, monthly debt payments / gross monthly income.
lines.say: The last number helps decide approval: D T I, your monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income.

lines.text: Example: $12,000 a month of income. The $3,346.52 bill is 27.9%. Add an $800 car loan: 34.6%.
lines.say: With twelve thousand dollars a month of income, our housing bill is twenty-seven point nine percent. Add an eight hundred dollar car payment, and it's thirty-four point six.

lines.text: Fannie Mae allows up to 50% DTI through its automated system, 36% to 45% underwritten by hand.
lines.say: Fannie Mae allows up to fifty percent through its automated system, and thirty-six to forty-five percent underwritten by hand. That's a ceiling, not a budget.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: Early payments are mostly interest: 89% of payment one in our example.
lines.say: Early payments are mostly interest: eighty-nine percent of payment one, in our example.

lines.text: The APR adds fees to the rate, which makes it useful for comparing offers.
lines.say: The A P R adds fees to the rate, which makes it useful for comparing offers.

lines.text: The real bill is PITI, and taxes and insurance can rise even on a fixed rate.
lines.say: The real bill is PITI, and taxes and insurance can rise even on a fixed rate.

lines.text: And PMI isn't forever: ask at 80%, automatic at 78%.
lines.say: And P M I isn't forever: you can ask at eighty percent, and it's automatic at seventy-eight.

lines.say: Remember: eighty-nine percent of that first payment went to interest. Now you know why.

post.title: Your first mortgage payment can be 89% interest. Every mortgage number, explained
post.ig: The first mortgage payment can be 89% interest. Here is every number on a mortgage, explained with real math.
post.tiktok: On a $400K loan at 7.40%, 89% of payment one is interest. Every mortgage number, explained.
post.yt_desc:
On a $400,000, 30-year loan at 7.40% (Freddie Mac's average on Oct 8, 2026), $2,466.67 of the first $2,769.52 payment is interest, and principal doesn't overtake interest until year 21. This video explains every number on a mortgage from zero: principal, interest rate versus APR, points and break-even, the amortization formula with exact math, total interest over 30 years, and 15-year versus 30-year loans. It then covers Freddie Mac's rate survey from 2016 to 2025, the 2026 conforming loan limit, PITI (property taxes, homeowners insurance, PMI and escrow), when PMI must end under the Homeowners Protection Act, closing costs, fixed versus adjustable-rate loans and debt-to-income ratios. All examples are hypothetical and labeled.

CHAPTERS

Sources: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey (Oct 8, 2026; annual averages 2016-2025; record high Oct 1981, record low Jan 2021); NAR Existing-Home Sales (Oct 13, 2026); FHFA 2026 conforming loan limits (Nov 2025); CFPB on APR, points, PMI cancellation and the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure; Regulation X (escrow); ATTOM 2025 property tax analysis (Apr 2026); Bankrate homeowners insurance (2026); Freddie Mac on PMI cost and closing costs; Fannie Mae Selling Guide (DTI); lender 5/6 SOFR ARM disclosures. Payment math is our own calculation with the standard amortization formula.

News and education, not financial advice.
